title: Pope Leo XIV Draws 700,000 to Paris Mass, Calls Young People 'Today's Church'
summary:
An estimated 700,000 people filled the Place de la Concorde in Paris on Saturday for an open-air Mass led by Pope Leo XIV — one of the largest gatherings of his four-day visit to France.

The event began with the pontiff riding down the Champs-Élysées Avenue in his open-topped popemobile, waving to dense crowds. Along the way, he blessed a number of young children as he travelled toward the square. He then celebrated Mass from a special altar on the Place de la Concorde. It was the second day of his trip.

In his homily, the Pope told worshippers that Catholics should not keep their faith private but should "let it overflow so that those you meet may be refreshed." He also addressed young people directly, calling them "today's Church." "How beautiful it is to see your enthusiasm, energy and commitment, and the joy you bring to Christian communities," he said.

Many senior politicians attended, including French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu and Brigitte Macron, the president's wife. Senate President Gérard Larcher was also seen at the Mass. President Emmanuel Macron did not attend and will not be at any of the Pope's Masses, largely to avoid appearing to breach France's strict rules on the separation of church and state. Several candidates for next year's presidential election were also spotted, including Marine Le Pen of the hard-right National Rally, conservative Bruno Retailleau, and centrists Édouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal.

Earlier on Saturday, the Pope visited the Maison Bakhita centre, which supports refugees, and praised the organization for inviting people to see "those who are invisible." He also stressed the "fundamental role of women in building a civilization of love." On Friday, he met Macron and joined 80,000 young people at the Stade de France. He also warned about the dangers of artificial intelligence. Large crowds are expected throughout the rest of his trip, which the Church believes reflects growing spirituality in France and Europe.
why_it_matters: The size of the crowd and the careful behaviour of France's politicians show how much is at stake in debates over religion's place in public life — and how young people are increasingly being courted as the future of both churches and political movements.

background_read: Pope Leo XIV (the head of the Roman Catholic Church worldwide, elected in 2025 and the first pope from the United States) was making a four-day visit to France, with the Paris Mass as its centrepiece.

France has some of the strictest church–state rules in Europe: a law passed in 1905 made the state officially non-religious, which is why French politicians are careful about how they appear at religious events such as papal Masses.

The Place de la Concorde, where the Mass was held, is one of Paris's largest public squares — during the French Revolution in the 1790s, the guillotine stood there and King Louis XVI was executed on the site.

The Champs-Élysées (the wide avenue that runs through central Paris toward the Arc de Triomphe) is normally used for national celebrations and parades, and the Stade de France (the country's national stadium, built for the 1998 football World Cup) hosted the 80,000 young people the day before.
Papal Masses in Paris are rare: Pope John Paul II drew enormous crowds to the city in 1997 for World Youth Day, and recent popes have more often visited other French cities rather than the capital.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — the Church and its supporters
perspectives.description: They read 700,000 people at a Mass, plus 80,000 young people at the Stade de France, as evidence of renewed energy in European Catholicism, especially among the young. The Pope's message that young people are 'today's Church' gives them a recognised role rather than a future one.

Supporters of France's strict separation of church and state worry that a huge public Mass at a national square blurs the line between religion and the state. They point out that even the president's absence was a political calculation, showing how much pressure the visit puts on that rule.

The presence of Marine Le Pen, Bruno Retailleau, Édouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal suggests the visit is being used as a stage before France's next presidential election, with candidates competing for Catholic and conservative voters while still respecting secular rules.

The trip's focus on refugees, the role of women and the risks of artificial intelligence hints at the issues the Church wants to be associated with in the coming years. Whether the crowds translate into lasting commitment among young Europeans is the real test.
